groups.name: Positioning, navigation and timing
groups.intro: Where GNSS receivers lose accuracy, are fed false positions, or are told to expect trouble, and how to tell deliberate interference from natural causes.

groups.name: Emitters seen from space
groups.intro: Transmitters that show up in satellite radar data as interference inside the radar's own band.

groups.name: Satellite communications
groups.intro: Open data can't see satcom jamming directly, so this half is built from orbits, outages, the official record and predictable natural effects.

groups.name: Context and assessment
groups.intro: Turning lane outputs into graded events with a stated basis, and keeping natural and benign explanations in view.

groups.name: Platform
groups.intro: How the outputs reach people: a public, licence-clean map and a private watch kept apart from it.

lanes.name: GNSS degradation from ADS-B
lanes.summary: Share of aircraft per area whose own GNSS accuracy degraded, by day, hour and minute.
lanes.what: Aircraft broadcast their own position quality (NACp and NIC). The processor turns a day of worldwide ADS-B into the share of aircraft in each H3 hex (about 1,770 km²) that lost accuracy, at two thresholds: worse than 93 m (jamming-scale loss) and worse than 10 m for aircraft that showed 10 m capability that day (space weather and SBAS problems).
lanes.how: Version-2 reports from the aircraft's own GNSS only, airborne, sampled at most every 30 s. A peer test drops faulty avionics, which are bad where their neighbours are fine. A post-exposure tag separates aircraft still degraded after leaving a jammed area. The hex score uses the formula GPSJam publishes, and hexes are coloured only with 5 or more aircraft.
lanes.notes: An effect measure, not attribution. Processing takes 53–70 s per worldwide day on one PC. Validated on 20 days (Oct–Nov 2025 and Sep 2026).

lanes.name: SBAS outage and storm flags
lanes.summary: Hours when an SBAS service area loses 10 m accuracy, labelled storm or probable service problem.
lanes.what: For each SBAS service area and UTC hour, the share of 10 m-capable aircraft that fell below 10 m. An hour is flagged as an outage at 60% or more and as degraded at 35% or more.
lanes.how: GFZ Kp of 5 or more labels a flagged hour as a storm; otherwise it is a probable service problem. Flagged hours are kept out of the 10 m baselines.
lanes.notes: Reconstructed the 13–17 Oct 2025 EGNOS outage to within an hour at both ends. On the 12 Nov 2025 G4 storm, 38.5% of capable aircraft fell below 10 m against a 3.7% baseline, while jamming-scale loss stayed flat.

lanes.name: Minute bursts and anomaly events
lanes.summary: Short interference bursts timed to the minute, and departures from each area's own baseline.
lanes.what: Per-minute counts of aircraft with gross-bad reports catch bursts that an hourly majority rule would dampen. Each region and hour is also compared with the same hour on up to 14 earlier days.
lanes.how: An anomaly is a share above the median by more than the larger of a fixed floor and 4 × MAD, with at least 30 aircraft-hex-hours behind it.
lanes.notes: Recovered both bursts of the 22 Sep 2026 San Francisco Bay Area GPS loss (18:00–18:08Z and 19:52–20:12Z). The NOTAM for that window is UNVERIFIED: it needs FAA NOTAM API access.

lanes.name: Downstream effects by aircraft type
lanes.summary: Which aircraft types stay degraded after leaving interference, and how far they carry it.
lanes.what: Some avionics keep reporting degraded accuracy for hours after an aircraft leaves a jammed or spoofed area. Over 17 days, A350-900s made up 24.9% of post-exposure aircraft-days against 1.3% of traffic (19.4×), A380s 19.2× and 777-300ERs 4.7×; most narrowbodies were near 1×.
lanes.how: An aircraft's exposure point is its first degraded hex-hour where its peers were degraded too. Later degraded reports 300 km or more away, among healthy peers, are tagged post-exposure.
lanes.notes: Hypothesis, not verified: some avionics reject GPS for the rest of a flight after spoofing exposure. Comparing against all traffic mixes route with type, so a like-for-like comparison is next. Airbus and EASA guidance hasn't been checked yet. Planned as a product for operators.

lanes.name: Radio-horizon jammer localizer
lanes.summary: Narrow down where a jammer sits from the first position at which each aircraft lost GNSS.
lanes.what: A jammer on the ground can only reach aircraft above its radio horizon. Each aircraft's first jammed position and altitude define a horizon circle, and where many circles' edges meet points to the source area.
lanes.how: Reuses the processor's per-aircraft exposure tracking. The method follows the open-source work that placed the 2024 Baltic jammer in Kaliningrad from aircraft data alone.
lanes.notes: Gives an area, not a site: the 2024 work was confident about the country, not an exact location.

lanes.name: ADS-B spoofing detection
lanes.summary: Aircraft fed false positions: jumps, convergence on false points, altitude mismatches.
lanes.what: Spoofing shows up as position jumps, many aircraft converging on the same false point, and divergence between GNSS (geometric) and barometric altitude.
lanes.how: Published detection methods applied to the same daily ADS-B stream, with the same peer and post-exposure logic.
lanes.notes: Kept separate from jamming in outputs, because the operational effect differs.

lanes.name: Spoofing at sea (AIS)
lanes.summary: Ship position reports that jump, circle or land ashore.
lanes.what: Ships broadcast GNSS-derived positions over AIS. Spoofed fixes appear as impossible tracks, ships placed on land and clusters in patterns.
lanes.how: Open AIS feeds in the Baltic and along the Norwegian coast, screened with the same effect-first approach as the aircraft lane.
data: Kystverket AIS (NLOD; licence text not yet read)
lanes.notes: Coverage is regional, not worldwide.

lanes.name: Declared interference and test notices
lanes.summary: What authorities say: navigation warnings, GPS test notices and NOTAMs.
lanes.what: Official notices that GNSS may be unreliable in an area and time window: maritime navigation warnings, US GPS interference test notices, NOTAMs and announced test events.
lanes.how: Light pollers on a schedule. A declared window becomes an explanation for observed degradation, or flags it as a planned test rather than an incident.
data: NGA Maritime Safety Information broadcast warnings
US Coast Guard NAVCEN GPS test notices
UKMTO advisories (reuse terms UNVERIFIED; private watch only)
lanes.notes: Pollers were prototyped in an earlier tool and will be ported to Cloudflare Workers cron. Announced events such as Jammertest serve as planned-test exclusions and known positives.

lanes.name: Space-weather context
lanes.summary: Geomagnetic storms and ionospheric scintillation, to separate natural degradation from deliberate interference.
lanes.what: Storms and scintillation degrade GNSS too. The Kp index already labels SBAS flags. ESA's worldwide scintillation nowcast (S4, sigma-phi and TEC on a 2.5° grid) is being archived hourly, because ESA keeps only the current hour.
lanes.how: Context layers sit beside the observed lanes. Thresholds follow ICAO's scintillation categories (S4 0.5/0.8, sigma-phi 0.4/0.7 rad).
data: ESA Space Weather Service Network scintillation nowcast (ESA S2P terms)
NOAA SWPC and GloTEC (US public domain)
lanes.notes: The ESA terms allow derived products with attribution, but the raw grids may be passed on only to people who accept the same terms, so the archive itself stays private. 'Data provided by the European Space Agency (ESA) as part of its Space Safety Programme (S2P)'.

lanes.name: L-band emitters from NISAR radar
lanes.summary: Transmitters inside NISAR's L-band receive slices (one contains GPS L2), from the processor's own RFI tables.
lanes.what: NISAR's L-band radar listens in 1219–1239 MHz (contains GPS L2) and 1291–1296 MHz over most land. Its processor records, for every block of raw data, how much interference it found and at which frequencies, before filtering it out.
lanes.how: Two detectors run on those tables. Tones: frequencies hit in most pulses, excluding the radar's own two tones. Broadband: the cross-polarized channel far above what the ground produces, the signature of a noise jammer. Positions come from the orbit, and a cheap first pass on the processor's score decides which passes get the full read.
data: NISAR L1 RSLC and L2 GCOV via ASF DAAC (NASA data, CC0 unless marked)
lanes.notes: The broadband detector passed its first positive control: an area with documented L1/L2/L5 jamming was detected on 12 of 13 passes that covered it. The published Shiraz jammer was not confirmed by either detector, and the earlier image-based method failed that test. Outputs stay private until validated. Credit to @auonsson, whose post prompted the idea.

lanes.name: Sentinel-1 RFI board
lanes.summary: C-band emitters from the interference reports in Sentinel-1 radar products.
lanes.what: Sentinel-1 Level-1 products carry per-burst radio-frequency-interference annotations. Mapped over time, they show persistent and new C-band emitters.
lanes.how: Same pattern as the NISAR lane: read only the annotations, never the imagery, and group detections into sites across passes.
lanes.notes: Needs a Copernicus Data Space account.

lanes.name: Weather-radar spokes
lanes.summary: Interference spokes in open weather-radar data, as evidence of nearby emitters.
lanes.what: A strong emitter in a weather radar's band paints a thin radial spoke on its scans. National services publish the scans.
lanes.how: Detect spokes, triangulate where several radars see the same source, and track persistence.
lanes.notes: C-band, so it complements the L-band NISAR lane.

lanes.name: Spaceborne and network GNSS
lanes.summary: GNSS reflectometry, radio occultation, ground reference networks and L-band radiometers.
lanes.what: CYGNSS GNSS-reflectometry has been used to localize a jammer (the Shiraz case). COSMIC-2 radio-occultation amplitude can indicate ground jamming power. CORS/IGS ground stations record degradation at fixed sites, and SMOS/SMAP map 1.4 GHz interference.
lanes.how: Each as its own lane, cross-checked against the aircraft and radar lanes.
data: ESA SMOS, NASA SMAP (licences UNVERIFIED for these products)
lanes.notes: Licences are checked and recorded before any of these feeds a layer.

lanes.name: Low-frequency navigation and VLF
lanes.summary: Chayka (Loran-type) and RSDN-20 Alpha VLF signals, the backups to GNSS.
lanes.what: Long-range terrestrial navigation systems matter more when GNSS is denied. Public receivers and direction-finding work make their activity observable.
lanes.how: Follow published receiver captures and VLF direction-finding methods; add public KiwiSDR receivers.
data: Public Loran/Chayka receiver captures (reuse terms UNVERIFIED; private watch only)
lanes.notes: Kept in the private watch until reuse terms are confirmed.

lanes.name: GEO threat board
lanes.summary: Known inspector satellites near commercial comsats, with drift and manoeuvre flags.
lanes.what: Daily positions of known GEO inspector satellites, such as the Olymp-K (Luch) and Shijian series, against the communications satellites near them.
lanes.how: Longitude-drift and manoeuvre flags from public orbital elements. Proximity thresholds are no tighter than public element accuracy (about 50 km).
lanes.notes: Shows proximity and behaviour, never intent.

lanes.name: Interference register
lanes.summary: Curated, geolocated cases of harmful interference from the official record.
lanes.what: Cases from ITU Radio Regulations Board decisions and operator disclosures, each geolocated where possible and cited to its source.
lanes.how: Hand-curated with a fixed record format; new RRB meetings are checked as they publish.
data: ITU RRB documents (cited, not republished; reuse terms UNVERIFIED)
lanes.notes: Doubles as a validation set for the observed lanes.

lanes.name: Satellite-internet health
lanes.summary: Telling a constellation-wide outage from a local one.
lanes.what: Internet-measurement data shows when satellite-ISP users in one area lose service while others don't.
lanes.how: Speed-test and outage-detection data, compared across areas and with the observed GNSS lanes.
data: RIPE Atlas (permission needed for commercial use)
lanes.notes: Permission requests to IODA and RIPE NCC go out before those sources are used.

lanes.name: L-band risk overlay
lanes.summary: Where observed GNSS jamming lies near L-band mobile-satellite services.
lanes.what: GNSS jammers and nearby L-band satcom (Inmarsat, Iridium, Thuraya) share spectrum neighbourhoods. This layer marks where observed jamming could plausibly affect them.
lanes.how: An inference layer built from the observed GNSS lanes and service frequencies.
lanes.notes: Labelled as inference on the map, never as observed satcom interference.

lanes.name: Sun-outage calculator
lanes.summary: Predictable daily losses when the sun passes behind a GEO satellite, to the minute.
lanes.what: Twice a year the sun sits behind each GEO satellite as seen from a given receiver, and dishes lose the signal for a few minutes a day. Losses inside those windows are natural; losses outside them deserve a second look.
lanes.how: A low-precision solar ephemeris (Meeus, about 0.01°), an ideal geostationary satellite and a WGS84 receiver. An outage is the sun within 1.2° of the satellite, which suits a 0.9 m Ku-band dish.
lanes.notes: Checked against an independently written calculator: the Tehran windows and times agree.

lanes.name: Events and grading
lanes.summary: Fusing lanes into events, each graded on five fields.
lanes.what: An event joins what the lanes saw in one place and time window. It is graded on signal type, support, localization, attribution and verdict.
lanes.how: One event model for every lane, stored with its evidence and sources. Grades state their basis: observed, declared or natural.
lanes.notes: Grades describe evidence strength. They don't name perpetrators.

lanes.name: Attribution and exclusion layers
lanes.summary: Benign explanations kept in view: licensed transmitters, radars, navaids, ducting.
lanes.what: Before an observation is treated as interference, check it against licensed transmitters, weather radars, navigation aids, space weather and tropospheric ducting.
lanes.how: Each layer is a lookup at the event's place and time. Ducting comes from reanalysis (ERA5).
data: Licensing and navaid databases (terms vary; checked per source)
lanes.notes: Known false look-alikes, such as radar faults, are kept as test cases.

lanes.name: Community reporting lane
lanes.summary: What researchers and operators report in public posts, collected daily as leads.
lanes.what: Public posts from researchers who track interference often come before any official notice. Bluesky and RSS/Atom collectors run daily into private digests.
lanes.how: Collected text is treated as data, never as instructions. Extraction will run through a least-privilege assistant task that can't see the watch configuration.
lanes.notes: The account and keyword lists are private. Posts are leads, never evidence on their own.

lanes.name: Daily status and weekly assessment
lanes.summary: A per-region daily status and a written weekly assessment.
lanes.what: Each region gets a daily status that says what it rests on (observed, declared, natural), and a weekly written assessment pulls the lanes together.
lanes.how: Built on the event model. Alerts go out through ntfy with generic text and no places.
lanes.notes: Products cite their sources and flag anything unverified.

lanes.name: Public map and data
lanes.summary: A daily map of GNSS degradation with a time slider and downloadable hex data.
lanes.what: A static site: MapLibre with H3 hexes, a time slider, the method card and the validation report. Daily hex data is downloadable under ODbL.
lanes.how: A daily pipeline in GitHub Actions, and a backfill from Oct 2025 (about 1.3 TB downloaded and discarded; only MBs a day are kept).
data: adsb.lol daily archive (ODbL; derived data published under ODbL with attribution)
lanes.notes: Static files on the free tier: no servers and no database bill.

lanes.name: Private watch
lanes.summary: Daily runs over private areas of interest, behind a login, kept apart from the public site.
lanes.what: Watch areas, keywords and alert history are private. The NISAR lane runs daily over a private area and publishes to a page behind Cloudflare Access.
lanes.how: Private configuration never enters the public repo; a check on every commit blocks private terms.
data: Same sources as the public lanes
lanes.notes: Event and alert state will move to Cloudflare D1 (free tier).
